entries.acf9b9de3e4684d6b8be61eaf2c2722cc9e455d6: <div sID="gen6422" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="22" osisID="2Sam.22" sID="2Sam.22"/> <div eID="gen6422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6423" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen6424" type="x-p"/> This chapter is a psalm, a psalm of praise; we find it afterwards inserted among David's psalms (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.1-Ps.18.50">Ps. xviii.</reference>) with some little variation. We have it here as it was first composed for his own closed and his own harp; but there we have it as it was afterwards delivered to the chief musician for the service of the church, a second edition with some amendments; for, though it was calculated primarily for David's case, yet it might indifferently serve the devotion of others, in giving thanks for their deliverances; or it was intended that his people should thus join with him in his thanksgivings, because, being a public person, his deliverances were to be accounted public blessings and called for public acknowledgments. The inspired historian, having largely related David's deliverances in this and the foregoing book, and one particularly in the close of the foregoing chapter, thought fit to record this sacred poem as a memorial of all that had been before related. Some think that David penned this psalm when he was old, upon a general review of the mercies of his life and the many wonderful preservations God had blessed him with, from first to last. We should in our praises, look as far back as we can, and not suffer time to wear out the sense of God's favours. Others think that he penned it when he was young, upon occasion of some of his first deliverances, and kept it by him for his use afterwards, and that, upon every new deliverance, his practice was to sing this song. But the book of Psalms shows that he varied as there was occasion, and confined not himself to one form. Here is, I. The title of the psalm, <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.1">ver. 1</reference>. II. The psalm itself, in which, with a very warm devotion and very great fluency and copiousness of expression, 1. He gives glory to God. 2. He takes comfort in him; and he finds matter for both, (1.) In the experiences he had of God's former favours. (2.) In the expectations he had of his further favours. These are intermixed throughout the whole psalm. <div eID="gen6424" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen6423" type="introduction"/>
entries.bbb6cc47c705b1352078b6e4cb256d46485efb47: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15"/><title type="x-s3">David's Song of Praise. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1020.)</title> <div sID="gen6425" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And David spake unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> the words of this song in the day <hi type="italic">that</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> had delivered him out of the hand of all his enemies, and out of the hand of Saul: <div eID="gen6425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6426" type="x-p"/> Observe here, I. That it has often been the lot of God's people to have many enemies, and to be in imminent danger of falling into their hands. David was a man after God's heart, but not after men's heart: many were those that hated him, and sought his ruin; Saul is particularly named, either, 1. As distinguished from his enemies of the heathen nations. Saul hated David, but David did not hate Saul, and therefore would not reckon him among his enemies; or, rather, 2. As the chief of his enemies, who was more malicious and powerful than any of them. Let not those whom God loves marvel if the world hate them. <div eID="gen6426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6427" type="x-p"/> II. Those that trust God in the way of duty shall find him a present help to them in their greatest dangers. David did so. God delivered him out of the hand of Saul. He takes special notice of this. Remarkable preservations should be mentioned in our praises with a particular emphasis. He delivered him also <hi type="italic">out of the hand of all his enemies,</hi> one after another, sometimes in one way, sometimes in another; and David, from his own experience, has assured us <hi type="italic">that, though many are the troubles of the righteous, yet the Lord delivers them out of them all,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.34.19">Ps. xxxiv. 19</reference>. We shall never be delivered from all our enemies till we get to heaven; and to that heavenly kingdom God will preserve all that are his, <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.18">2 Tim. iv. 18</reference>. <div eID="gen6427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6428" type="x-p"/> III. Those that have received many signal mercies from God ought to give him the glory of them. Every new mercy in our hand should put a new song into our mouth, even praises to our God. Where there is a grateful heart, out of the abundance of that the mouth will speak. David spoke, not only to himself, for his own pleasure, not merely to those about him, for their instruction, but <hi type="italic">to the Lord,</hi> for his honour, <hi type="italic">the words of this song.</hi> Then we sing with grace when we sing to the Lord. In distress he <hi type="italic">cried with his voice</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.142.1">Ps. cxlii. 1</reference>), therefore with his voice he gave thanks. Thanksgiving to God is the sweetest vocal music. <div eID="gen6428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6429" type="x-p"/> IV. We ought to be speedy in our thankful returns to God: <hi type="italic">In the day that God delivered him he sang this song.</hi> While the mercy is fresh, and our devout affections are most excited by it, let the thank-offering be brought, that it may be kindled with the fire of those affections. <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15"/> <div eID="gen6429" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">David's Thanksgiving. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1020.)</title> <div sID="gen6430" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">2</hi> And he said, The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer; <hi type="super">3</hi> The God of my rock; in him will I trust: <hi type="italic">he is</hi> my shield, and the horn of my salvation, my high tower, and my refuge, my saviour; thou savest me from violence. <hi type="super">4</hi> I will call on the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , <hi type="italic">who is</hi> worthy to be praised: so shall I be saved from mine enemies. <hi type="super">5</hi> When the waves of death compassed me, the floods of ungodly men made me afraid; <hi type="super">6</hi> The sorrows of hell compassed me about; the snares of death prevented me; <hi type="super">7</hi> In my distress I called upon the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and cried to my God: and he did hear my voice out of his temple, and my cry <hi type="italic">did enter</hi> into his ears. <hi type="super">8</hi> Then the earth shook and trembled; the foundations of heaven moved and shook, because he was wroth. <hi type="super">9</hi> There went up a smoke out of his nostrils, and fire out of his mouth devoured: coals were kindled by it. <hi type="super">10</hi> He bowed the heavens also, and came down; and darkness <hi type="italic">was</hi> under his feet. <hi type="super">11</hi> And he rode upon a cherub, and did fly: and he was seen upon the wings of the wind. <hi type="super">12</hi> And he made darkness pavilions round about him, dark waters, <hi type="italic">and</hi> thick clouds of the skies. <hi type="super">13</hi> Through the brightness before him were coals of fire kindled. <hi type="super">14</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thundered from heaven, and the most High uttered his voice. <hi type="super">15</hi> And he sent out arrows, and scattered them; lightning, and discomfited them. <hi type="super">16</hi> And the channels of the sea appeared, the foundations of the world were discovered, at the rebuking of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , at the blast of the breath of his nostrils. <hi type="super">17</hi> He sent from above, he took me; he drew me out of many waters; <hi type="super">18</hi> He delivered me from my strong enemy, <hi type="italic">and</hi> from them that hated me: for they were too strong for me. <hi type="super">19</hi> They prevented me in the day of my calamity: but the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> was my stay. <hi type="super">20</hi> He brought me forth also into a large place: he delivered me, because he delighted in me. <hi type="super">21</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> rewarded me according to my righteousness: according to the cleanness of my hands hath he recompensed me. <hi type="super">22</hi> For I have kept the ways of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and have not wickedly departed from my God. <hi type="super">23</hi> For all his judgments <hi type="italic">were</hi> before me: and <hi type="italic">as for</hi> his statutes, I did not depart from them. <hi type="super">24</hi> I was also upright before him, and have kept myself from mine iniquity. <hi type="super">25</hi> Therefore the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath recompensed me according to my righteousness; according to my cleanness in his eye sight. <hi type="super">26</hi> With the merciful thou wilt shew thyself merciful, <hi type="italic">and</hi> with the upright man thou wilt shew thyself upright. <hi type="super">27</hi> With the pure thou wilt shew thyself pure; and with the froward thou wilt shew thyself unsavoury. <hi type="super">28</hi> And the afflicted people thou wilt save: but thine eyes <hi type="italic">are</hi> upon the haughty, <hi type="italic">that</hi> thou mayest bring <hi type="italic">them</hi> down. <hi type="super">29</hi> For thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> my lamp, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> : and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will lighten my darkness. <hi type="super">30</hi> For by thee I have run through a troop: by my God have I leaped over a wall. <hi type="super">31</hi> <hi type="italic">As for</hi> God, his way <hi type="italic">is</hi> perfect; the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> tried: he <hi type="italic">is</hi> a buckler to all them that trust in him. <hi type="super">32</hi> For who <hi type="italic">is</hi> God, save the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ? and who <hi type="italic">is</hi> a rock, save our God? <hi type="super">33</hi> God <hi type="italic">is</hi> my strength <hi type="italic">and</hi> power: and he maketh my way perfect. <hi type="super">34</hi> He maketh my feet like hinds' <hi type="italic">feet:</hi> and setteth me upon my high places. <hi type="super">35</hi> He teacheth my hands to war; so that a bow of steel is broken by mine arms. <hi type="super">36</hi> Thou hast also given me the shield of thy salvation: and thy gentleness hath made me great. <hi type="super">37</hi> Thou hast enlarged my steps under me; so that my feet did not slip. <hi type="super">38</hi> I have pursued mine enemies, and destroyed them; and turned not again until I had consumed them. <hi type="super">39</hi> And I have consumed them, and wounded them, that they could not arise: yea, they are fallen under my feet. <hi type="super">40</hi> For thou hast girded me with strength to battle: them that rose up against me hast thou subdued under me. <hi type="super">41</hi> Thou hast also given me the necks of mine enemies, that I might destroy them that hate me. <hi type="super">42</hi> They looked, but <hi type="italic">there was</hi> none to save; <hi type="italic">even</hi> unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , but he answered them not. <hi type="super">43</hi> Then did I beat them as small as the dust of the earth, I did stamp them as the mire of the street, <hi type="italic">and</hi> did spread them abroad. <hi type="super">44</hi> Thou also hast delivered me from the strivings of my people, thou hast kept me <hi type="italic">to be</hi> head of the heathen: a people <hi type="italic">which</hi> I knew not shall serve me. <hi type="super">45</hi> Strangers shall submit themselves unto me: as soon as they hear, they shall be obedient unto me. <hi type="super">46</hi> Strangers shall fade away, and they shall be afraid out of their close places. <hi type="super">47</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> liveth; and blessed <hi type="italic">be</hi> my rock; and exalted be the God of the rock of my salvation. <hi type="super">48</hi> It <hi type="italic">is</hi> God that avengeth me, and that bringeth down the people under me, <hi type="super">49</hi> And that bringeth me forth from mine enemies: thou also hast lifted me up on high above them that rose up against me: thou hast delivered me from the violent man. <hi type="super">50</hi> Therefore I will give thanks unto thee, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , among the heathen, and I will sing praises unto thy name. <hi type="super">51</hi> <hi type="italic">He is</hi> the tower of salvation for his king: and sheweth mercy to his anointed, unto David, and to his seed for evermore. <div eID="gen6430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6431" type="x-p"/> Let us observe, in this song of praise, <div eID="gen6431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6432" type="x-p"/> I. How David adores God, and gives him the glory of his infinite perfections. There is none like him, nor any to be compared with him (<reference osisRef="2Sam.22.32">v. 32</reference>): <hi type="italic">Who is God, save the Lord?</hi> All others that are adored as deities are counterfeits and pretenders. None is to be relied on but he. <hi type="italic">Who is a rock, save our God?</hi> They are dead, but <hi type="italic">the Lord liveth,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.47">v. 47</reference>. They disappoint their worshippers when they most need them. But <hi type="italic">as for God his way is perfect,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.31">v. 31</reference>. Men begin in kindness, but end not-promise, but perform not; but God will finish his work, and his word is tried, and what we may trust. <div eID="gen6432" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6433" type="x-p"/> II. How he triumphs in the interest he has in this God, and his relation to him, which he lays down as the foundation of all the benefits he has received from him: <hi type="italic">He is my God;</hi> as such he cries to him (<reference osisRef="2Sam.22.7">v. 7</reference>), and cleaves to him (<reference osisRef="2Sam.22.22">v. 22</reference>); "and, if <hi type="italic">my God,</hi> then <hi type="italic">my rock</hi>" (<reference osisRef="2Sam.22.2">v. 2</reference>), that is, "my strength and my power (<reference osisRef="2Sam.22.33">v. 33</reference>), the rock under which I take shelter (he who is to me as the shadow of a great rock in a weary land), the rock on which I build my hope," <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.3">v. 3</reference>. Whatever is my strength and support, it is <hi type="italic">the God of my rock that makes it so;</hi> nay, he is <hi type="italic">the God of the rock of my salvation</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.22.47">v. 47</reference>): my saving strength is in him and from him. David often hid himself in a rock (<reference osisRef="1Sam.24.2">1 Sam. xxiv. 2</reference>), but God was his chief hiding-place. "He is my fortress, in which I am safe and think myself so—<hi type="italic">my high tower,</hi> or stronghold, in which I am out of the reach of real evils—the <hi type="italic">tower of salvation</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.22.51">v. 51</reference>), which can never be sealed nor battered, nor undermined. Salvation itself saves me. Am I in distress? he is my deliverer—struck at, shot at? he is my shield—pursued? he is my refuge—oppressed? he is my saviour, that rescues me out of the hand of those that seek my ruin. Nay, he is the <hi type="italic">horn of my salvation,</hi> by which I am strongly protected, and my enemies are strongly pushed." Christ is spoken of as the <hi type="italic">horn of salvation</hi> in the house of David, <reference osisRef="Luke.1.69">Luke i. 69</reference>. "Am I burdened, and ready to sink? <hi type="italic">The Lord is my stay</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.22.19">v. 19</reference>), by whom I am supported. Am I in the dark, benighted, at a loss? <hi type="italic">Thou art my lamp, O Lord!</hi> to show me my way, and thou wilt dispel <hi type="italic">my darkness,</hi>" <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.29">v. 29</reference>. If we sincerely take the Lord for our God, all this, and much more, he will be to us, all we need and can desire. <div eID="gen6433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6434" type="x-p"/> III. What improvement he makes of his interest in God. If he be mine, 1. <hi type="italic">In him will I trust</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.22.3">v. 3</reference>), that is, "I will resign myself to his direction, and then depend upon his power, and wisdom, and goodness, to conduct me well." 2. <hi type="italic">On him I will call</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.22.4">v. 4</reference>), <hi type="italic">for he is worthy to be praised.</hi> What we have found in God that is worthy to be praised should engage us to pray to him and give glory to him. 3. <hi type="italic">To him will I give thanks</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.22.50">v. 50</reference>), and that publicly. When he was among the heathen he would neither be afraid nor ashamed to own his obligations to the God of Israel. <div eID="gen6434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6435" type="x-p"/> IV. The full and large account he keeps for himself, and gives to others, of the great and kind things God had done for him. This takes up most of the song. He gives God the glory both of his deliverances and of his successes, showing both the perils he was delivered from and the power he was advanced to. <div eID="gen6435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6436" type="x-p"/> 1. He magnifies the great salvations God had wrought for him. God sometimes brings his people into very great difficulties and dangers, that he may have the honour of saving them and they the comfort of being saved by him. He owns, <hi type="italic">Thou hast saved me from violence</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.22.3">v. 3</reference>), <hi type="italic">from my enemies</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.22.4">v. 4</reference>), <hi type="italic">from my strong enemy,</hi> meaning Saul, who, if God had not succoured him, would have been too hard for him, <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.18">v. 18</reference>. Thou hast given me <hi type="italic">the shield of thy salvation,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.36">v. 36</reference>. To magnify the salvation, he observes, <div eID="gen6436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6437" type="x-p"/> (1.) That the danger was very great and threatening out of which he was delivered. Men <hi type="italic">rose up against him</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.22.40">v. 40</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.49">49</reference>) that <hi type="italic">hated him</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.22.41">v. 41</reference>), <hi type="italic">a violent man</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.22.49">v. 49</reference>) namely, Saul, who was malicious in his designs against him and vigorous in his pursuit. This is expressed figuratively, <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.5-2Sam.22.6">v. 5, 6</reference>. He was surrounded with death on every side, threatened to be overwhelmed, and saw no way of escape. So violently did the waves of death beat upon him, so strongly did the cords and snares of death hold him, that he could not help himself, any more than a man in the grave can. The floods of Belial, the wicked one, and his wicked instruments, made him afraid; he trembled to see not only earth, but death and hell, in arms against him. <div eID="gen6437" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6438" type="x-p"/> (2.) That his deliverance was an answer to prayer, <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.7">v. 7</reference>. He has here left us a good example, when we are in distress, to cry unto God with importunity, as children in a fright cry to their parents; and great encouragement to do so, in that he found God ready to answer prayer out of his temple in heaven, where he is continually served and adored. <div eID="gen6438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6439" type="x-p"/> (3.) That God appeared in a singular and extraordinary manner for him and against his enemies. The expressions are borrowed from the descent of the divine Majesty upon Mount Sinai, <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.8-2Sam.22.9">v. 8, 9</reference>, &c. We do not find that in any of David's battles God fought for him with thunder (as in Samuel's time), or with hail (as in Joshua's time), or with the stars in their courses (as in Deborah's time); but these lofty metaphors are used, [1.] To set forth the glory of God, which was manifested in his deliverance. God's wisdom and power, his goodness and faithfulness, his justice and holiness, and his sovereign dominion over all the creatures and all the counsels of men, which appeared in favour of David, were as clear and bright a discovery of God's glory to an eye of faith as such miraculous interpositions would have been to an eye of sense. [2.] To set forth God's displeasure against his enemies, God so espoused his cause that he showed himself an enemy to all his enemies; his anger is set forth by a <hi type="italic">smoke out of his nostrils,</hi> and <hi type="italic">fire out of his mouth</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.22.9">v. 9</reference>), <hi type="italic">coals kindled</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.22.13">v. 13</reference>), <hi type="italic">arrows,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.15">v. 15</reference>. Who knows the power and terror of his wrath? [3.] To set forth the extraordinary confusion which his enemies were put into, and the consternation that seized them; as if the earth had trembled and the <hi type="italic">foundations of the world</hi> had been discovered, <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.8">v. 8</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.16">16</reference>. Who can stand before God when he is angry? [4.] To show how ready God was to help him: <hi type="italic">He rode upon a cherub and did fly,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.11">v. 11</reference>. God hastened to his succour, and came to him with seasonable relief, though he had seemed at a distance; yet he was <hi type="italic">a God hiding himself</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.15">Isa. xiv. 15</reference>), for he made <hi type="italic">darkness his pavilion</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.22.12">v. 12</reference>), for the amazement of his enemies and the protection of his own people. <div eID="gen6439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6440" type="x-p"/> (4.) That God manifested his particular favour and kindness to him in these deliverances (<reference osisRef="2Sam.22.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">He delivered me, because he delighted in me.</hi> The deliverance came not from common providence, but covenant-love; he was herein treated as a favourite: so he perceived by the communications of divine grace and comfort to his soul with these deliverances, and the communion he had with God in them. Herein he was a type of Christ, whom God upheld because he <hi type="italic">delighted in him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.42.1-Isa.42.2">Isa. xlii. 1, 2</reference>. <div eID="gen6440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6441" type="x-p"/> 2. He magnifies the great successes God had crowned him with. He had not only preserved but prospered him. He was blessed, (1.) With liberty and enlargement. He was <hi type="italic">brought into a large place</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.22.20">v. 20</reference>), where he had room to thrive, and his <hi type="italic">steps were enlarged under him,</hi> so that he had room to stir (<reference osisRef="2Sam.22.37">v. 37</reference>), being no longer straitened and confined. (2.) With military skill, and strength, and swiftness. Though he was bred up to the crook, he was well instructed in the arts of war and qualified for the toils and perils of it. God, having called him to fight his battles, qualified him for the service. He made him very ingenious (<hi type="italic">He teacheth my hands to war,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.35">v. 35</reference>. And this ingenuity was as good as strength, for it follows, "so <hi type="italic">that a bow of steel is broken by my arms,</hi>" not so much by main force as by dexterity), and very vigorous and valiant. (<hi type="italic">Thou hast girded me with strength to battle,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.40">v. 40</reference>. He gives God the glory of all his courage and ability for service), and very expeditious: <hi type="italic">He maketh my feet swift like hinds feet</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.22.34">v. 34</reference>), which is of great advantage both in charging and retreating. (3.) With victory over his enemies, not only Saul and Absalom, but the Philistines, Moabites, Ammonites, Syrians, and other neighbouring nations, whom he subdued and made tributaries to Israel. His wonderful victories are here described, <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.38-2Sam.22.43">v. 38-43</reference>. They were <hi type="italic">speedy</hi> victories (<hi type="italic">I turned not again till I had consumed them,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.38">v. 38</reference>) and <hi type="italic">complete</hi> victories. The enemies of Israel were <hi type="italic">wounded, destroyed, consumed,</hi> fell <hi type="italic">under his feet,</hi> trampled upon, and disabled to rise, and their necks lay at his mercy. They cried both to earth and heaven for help, but in vain. <hi type="italic">There was none to save,</hi> none that durst appear for them. God <hi type="italic">answered them, not</hi> for they were not on his side, nor did they cry unto him till they were brought to the last extremity. Being thus abandoned, they became an easy prey to David's righteous and victorious sword, so that he <hi type="italic">beat them as small as the dust of the earth,</hi> which is scattered by the wind and trodden on by every foot. (4.) With advancement to honour and power. To this he was anointed before his troubles began, and at length, <hi type="italic">post tot discrimina rerum—after all his dangers and disasters,</hi> he gained his point. God <hi type="italic">made his way perfect</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.22.33">v. 33</reference>), gave him success in all his undertakings, <hi type="italic">set him upon his high places</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.22.34">v. 34</reference>), denoting both safety and dignity. God's gentleness, his grace and tender mercy, <hi type="italic">made him great</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.22.36">v. 36</reference>), gave him great wealth, and great authority, and a name like that of the great men of the earth. He was <hi type="italic">kept to be the head of the heathen</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.22.44">v. 44</reference>); his signal preservations evinced that he was designed and reserved for something great—to rule over all Israel, notwithstanding the <hi type="italic">strivings of the people,</hi> and so that those whom <hi type="italic">he had not known should serve him,</hi> many of the nations that lay remote. Thus he was <hi type="italic">lifted up on high,</hi> as high as the throne, above those that <hi type="italic">rose up against him,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.49">v. 49</reference>. <div eID="gen6441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6442" type="x-p"/> V. The comfortable reflections he makes upon his own integrity, which God, by those wonderful deliverances, had graciously owned and witnessed to, <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.21-2Sam.22.25">v. 21-25</reference>. He means especially his integrity with reference to Saul and Ishbosheth, Absalom and Sheba, and those who either opposed his coming to the crown or endeavoured to dethrone him. They falsely accused him and misrepresented him, but he had the testimony of this conscience for him that he was not an ambitious aspiring man, a false and bloody man, as they called him,—that he had never taken any indirect unlawful courses to secure or raise himself, but in his whole conduct had kept in the way of his duty,—and that in the whole course of his conversation he had, for the main, made religion his business, so that he could take God's favours to him as the rewards of his righteousness, not of debt, but of grace. God had recompensed him, though not for his righteousness, as if that had merited any thing at the hand of God, yet according to his righteousness, which he was well pleased with, and had an eye to. His conscience witnessed for him, 1. That he had made the word of God his rule, and had kept to it, <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.23">v. 23</reference>. Wherever he was, God's judgments were before him as his guide; whithersoever he went, he took his religion along with him, and though he was forced to depart from his country, and sent, as it were, to serve other gods, yet as for God's statutes, he did not depart from them, but kept the way of the Lord and walked in it. 2. That he had carefully avoided the bye-paths of sin. He had not wickedly departed from his God. He could not say but that he had taken some false steps, but he had not deserted God, nor forsaken his way. Sins of infirmity he could not acquit himself from, but the grace of God had kept him from presumptuous sins. Though he had sometimes <hi type="italic">weakly</hi> departed from his God. By this it appeared that he was <hi type="italic">upright before God,</hi> or <hi type="italic">to God</hi> (in his sight, and with an eye to him), that he <hi type="italic">kept himself from his own iniquity,</hi> not only from that particular sin of killing Saul when it was in the power of his hand to do it, but, in general, he was afraid of sin and watchful against it, and made conscience of what he said and did. The matter of Uriah is an exception (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.5">1 Kings xv. 5</reference>), like that in Hezekiah's character, <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.31">2 Chron. xxxii. 31</reference>. Note, A careful abstaining from our own iniquity is one of the best evidences of our own integrity; and the testimony of our conscience for us that we have done so will be such a rejoicing as will not only lessen the griefs of an afflicted state, but increase the comforts of a prosperous state. David reflected with more comfort upon his victories over his own iniquity than upon his conquest of Goliath and all the hosts of the uncircumcised Philistines; and the witness of his own heart to his uprightness was sweeter though more silent music than theirs that sang, <hi type="italic">David has slain his ten thousands.</hi> If a great man be a good man, his goodness will be much more his satisfaction than his greatness. Let favour be shown to the upright and his uprightness will sweeten it, will double it. <div eID="gen6442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6443" type="x-p"/> VI. The comfortable prospects he has of God's further favour. As he looks back, so he looks forward, with pleasure, and assures himself of the kindness God has in store for all the saints, for himself, and also for his seed. <div eID="gen6443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6444" type="x-p"/> 1. For all good people, <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.26-2Sam.22.28">v. 26-28</reference>. As God had dealt with him according to his uprightness, so he will with all others. He takes occasion here to lay down the established rules of God's procedure with the children of men:— <div eID="gen6444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6445" type="x-p"/> (1.) That he will do good to those that are upright in their hearts. As we are found towards God, he will be found towards us. [1.] God's mercy and grace will be the joy of those that are merciful and gracious. Even the merciful need mercy; and they shall obtain it. [2.] God's uprightness, his justice and faithfulness, will be the joy of those that are upright, just, and faithful, both towards God and man. [3.] God's purity and holiness will be the joy of those that are pure and holy, who therefore give thanks at the remembrance thereof. And, if any of these good people be <hi type="italic">afflicted people, he will save</hi> them, either out of their afflictions or by and after them. On the other hand, <div eID="gen6445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6446" type="x-p"/> (2.) That those who turn aside to crooked ways he will <hi type="italic">lead forth with the workers of iniquity,</hi> as he says in another psalm. <hi type="italic">With the froward he will wrestle;</hi> and those with whom God wrestles are sure to be foiled. <hi type="italic">Woe unto him that strives with his Maker!</hi> God will walk contrary to those that walk contrary to him and be displeased with those that are displeased with him. As for the haughty, his eyes are upon them, marking them out, as it were, to be brought down; for <hi type="italic">he resists the proud.</hi> <div eID="gen6446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6447" type="x-p"/> 2. For himself. He foresaw that his conquests and kingdom would be yet further enlarged, <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.45-2Sam.22.46">v. 45, 46</reference>. Even the <hi type="italic">sons of the stranger,</hi> that would hear the report of his victories and the tokens of God's presence with him, would be possessed with a fear of him, would be forced to submit to him, though feignedly, and would be obedient to him. The successes which he had had he looked upon as earnests of more and means of more. Who durst oppose him by whom so many had been overcome? Thus the Son of David <hi type="italic">goes on conquering and to conquer,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.6.2">Rev. vi. 2</reference>. His gospel, which has been victorious, shall be so more and more. <div eID="gen6447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6448" type="x-p"/> 3. For his seed: He <hi type="italic">showeth mercy to his Messiah</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.22.51">v. 51</reference>), not only to David himself, but to that seed of his for evermore. David was himself anointed of God, not a usurper, but duly called to the government and qualified for it; therefore he doubted not but God would show mercy to him, that mercy which he had promised not to take from him nor from his posterity (<reference osisRef="2Sam.7.15-2Sam.7.16">ch. vii. 15, 16</reference>); on that promise he depends, with an eye to Christ, who alone is his <hi type="italic">seed for evermore,</hi> whose throne and kingdom still continue, and will to the end, whereas the seed and lineage of David are long since extinct. See <reference osisRef="Ps.89.28-Ps.89.29">Ps. lxxxix. 28, 29</reference>. Thus all his joys and all his hopes terminate, as ours should, in the great Redeemer.  <chapter eID="2Sam.22"/> <div eID="gen6448" type="x-p"/>

entries.6fddf449b6649affa2f4a9d66ea3d9fa73dedb12: <chapter n="22" osisID="2Sam.22" sID="2Sam.22"/><div eID="gen4211" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3041"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 22</title> <div sID="gen4212" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.1-2Sam.22.51">2Sa 22:1-51</reference>. David's Psalm of Thanksgiving for God's Powerful Deliverance and Manifold Blessings.<div eID="gen4212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4213" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">The song contained in this chapter is the same as the eighteenth Psalm, where the full commentary will be given [see on <reference osisRef="Ps.18.1">Psa 18:1</reference>, &c.]. It may be sufficient simply to remark that Jewish writers have noticed a great number of very minute variations in the language of the song as recorded here, from that embodied in the Book of Psalms--</hi>which may be accounted for by the fact that this, the first copy of the poem, was carefully revised and altered by David afterwards, when it was set to the music of the tabernacle. This inspired ode was manifestly the effusion of a mind glowing with the highest fervor of piety and gratitude, and it is full of the noblest imagery that is to be found within the range even of sacred poetry. It is David's grand tribute of thanksgiving for deliverance from his numerous and powerful enemies, and establishing him in the power and glory of the kingdom. <chapter eID="2Sam.22"/>

entries.310bd032e7fe8f980f91cc582987f5684517b7b9: <div eID="gen11324" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen11325" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11326" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11326" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11325" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11327" type="x-p"/> David's psalm of thanksgiving for God's powerful deliverance and manifold blessings, including prophetic declarations relative to the humiliation and exaltation of the Messiah, vv. 1-51. <div eID="gen11327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11328" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen11328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11329" type="x-p"/> David spake unto the Lord the words of this song - This is the same in substance, and almost in words, with Psalm 18:1-50, and therefore the exposition of it must be reserved till it occurs in its course in that book, with the exception of a very few observations, and Dr. Kennicott's general view of the subject.
entries.2d59928d33f522a18dfa3f847ba8e09b1d0734a2: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen11329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11330" type="x-p"/> When the waves of death compassed me - Though in a primary sense many of these things belong to David, yet generally and fully they belong to the Messiah alone.
entries.81de5008c2697bf24ccb3bcbaf7c5fe1d3b7ee59: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen11330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11331" type="x-p"/> He rode upon a cherub, and did fly - he was seen upon the things of the wind - In the original of this sublime passage, sense and sound are astonishingly well connected. I shall insert the Hebrew, represent it in English letters for the sake of the unlearned reader, and have only to observe, he must read from the right to the left. רוח כנפי על וירא ויעף כרוב על וירכב ruach canphey al vaiyera vaiyaoph kerub al vayirkab wind the of wings the upon seen was he and; fly did and cherub upon rode he <div eID="gen11331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11332" type="x-p"/> The clap of the wing, the agitation and rush through the air are expressed here in a very extraordinary manner. <div eID="gen11332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11333" type="x-p"/> Other beauties of this kind will be noted in the exposition of the Psalm alluded to above. <div eID="gen11333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11334" type="x-p"/> I now subjoin Dr. Kennicott's remarks on this chapter: - "The very sublime poetry contained in this chapter is universally admired, and yet it cannot be perfectly understood, till it is known Who is the speaker, who the person thus triumphant over mighty enemies, whose Sufferings occasioned such a dreadful convulsion of nature, and, who, upon his deliverance, inflicted such vengeance on his own people, and also became thus a king over the heathen. Should we be told that this person was David, it will be very difficult to show how this description can possibly agree with that character: but if it did in fact agree, yet would it contradict St. Paul, who quotes part of it as predicting the conversion of the Gentiles under Christ the Messiah. <reference osisRef="Rom.15.9">Rom 15:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.2.13">Heb 2:13</reference>; and see Peirce's Commentary, p. 50. Now if the person represented as speaking through this Divine ode be David only, the Messiah is excluded. In consequence of the difficulties resulting from each of these suppositions, the general idea has been that it relates both to David and to the Messiah as a prophecy of a double sense; first, as spoken by David of himself, and yet to be understood in a secondary sense, of the Messiah. But it must be remarked here, that if spoken only of David, it is not a prediction of any thing future, but a thanksgiving for favors past, and therefore is no prophecy at all. And farther, it could not be a prophecy descriptive of David unless the particulars agreed to David, which they evidently do not. If then David be here necessarily excluded from the single sense, he must be excluded also from the double sense, because nothing can be intended by any sacred writer, to relate to two persons, unless it be True of both; but it not being the case here as to David, we must conclude that this song relates only to the Messiah; and on this subject an excellent Dissertation, by the late Mr. Peirce, is subjoined to his comment on the Epistle to the Hebrews. It may be necessary to add here two remarks: the twenty-fourth verse now ends with, I have kept myself from mine iniquity, which words, it is objected, are not proper, if applied to the Messiah. But this difficulty is removed, in part, by the context, which represents the speaker as perfectly innocent and righteous; and this exactly agrees with the proof arising from the Syriac and Arabic versions, and also the Chaldee paraphrase, that this word was anciently מעונים ab iniquitatibus; consequently, this is one of the many instances where the ם final mem is improperly omitted by the Jewish transcribers. See my General Dissertation. Lastly, the difficulty arising from the title, which ascribes the Psalm to David, and which seems to make him the speaker in it, may be removed, either by supposing that the title here, like those now prefixed to several Psalms, is of no sufficient authority; or rather, by considering this title as only meant to describe the time when David composed this prophetic hymn, that when delivered from all his other enemies as well as from the hand of Saul, he then consecrated his leisure by composing this sublime prophecy concerning Messiah, his son, whom he represents here as speaking, (just as in Psalm 22, 40, and other places), and as describing, <div eID="gen11334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11335" type="x-p"/> 1. His triumph over death and hell; <div eID="gen11335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11336" type="x-p"/> 2. The manifestations of Omnipotence in his favor, earth and heaven, trembling at God's awful presence; <div eID="gen11336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11337" type="x-p"/> 3. The speaker's innocence thus divinely attested; <div eID="gen11337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11338" type="x-p"/> 4. The vengeance he was to take on his own people the Jews, in the destruction of Jerusalem; and, <div eID="gen11338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11339" type="x-p"/> 5. The adoption of the heathen, over whom he was to be the head and ruler. "Another instance of a title denoting only the time of a prophecy, occurs in the very next chapter; where a prophecy concerning the Messiah is entitled, The Last words of David; i.e., a hymn which he composed a little before his death, after all his other prophecies. And perhaps this ode in 2 Samuel 22, which immediately precedes that in 2 Samuel 23, was composed but a little while before; namely, when all his wars were over. Let it be added, that Josephus, immediately before he speaks of David's mighty men, which follow in this same chapter of Samuel, considers the two hymns in 2 Samuel 22 and 23, as both written after his wars were over - Jam Davides, bellis et periculis perfunctus, pacemque deinceps profundam agitans, odas in Deum hymnosque composuit. Tom. i., page 401."  <chapter eID="2Sam.22"/> <div eID="gen11339" type="x-p"/>

entries.ad4a843a49c78335e68d6e1f778d40cbe823e799: <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.1">2Sa 22:1</reference> <div eID="gen4563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4564" type="x-p"/> The heading is formed precisely according to the introductory formula of the song of Moses in <reference osisRef="Deut.31.30">Deu 31:30</reference>, and was no doubt taken from the larger historical work employed by the author of our books. It was probably also adopted from this into the canonical collection of the Psalter, and simply brought into conformity with the headings of the other psalms by the alteration of דּוד וידבּר (and David said) into דּבּר עשׁר לדוד יהוה לעבד (“Of David, the servant of the Lord, who spake:” Eng. ver.), and the insertion of למנצּח (“to the chief musician:” Eng. ver.) at the head (see Delitzsch on the Psalms). “<hi type="italic">In the day</hi>,” i.e., at the time, “<hi type="italic">when Jehovah had delivered him</hi>.” Deliverance “<hi type="italic">out of the hand of Saul</hi>” is specially mentioned, not because this was the last, but because it was the greatest and most glorious, - a deliverance out of the deepest misery into regal might and glory. The psalm is opened by ויּאמר in both texts. <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.2-2Sam.22.4">2Sa 22:2-4</reference> form the introduction.   2  Jehovah is my rock, my castle, and my deliverer to me;   3  My Rock-God, in whom I trust: <div eID="gen4564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4565" type="x-p"/> My shield and horn of my salvation, my fortress and my refuge, <div eID="gen4565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4566" type="x-p"/> My Saviour; from violence Thou redeemest me.   4  I call upon the praised one, Jehovah, <div eID="gen4566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4567" type="x-p"/> And I am saved from my enemies. <div eID="gen4567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4568" type="x-p"/> This introduction contains the sum and substance of the whole psalm, inasmuch as David groups the many experiences of divine deliverance in his agitated life into a long series of predicates, in all of which he extols God as his defence, refuge, and deliverer. The heaping up of these predicates is an expression both of liveliest gratitude, and also of hope for the future. The different predicates, however, are not to be taken as in apposition to <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi>, or as vocatives, but are declarations concerning God, how He had proved himself faithful to the Psalmist in all the calamities of his life, and would assuredly do so still. David calls God וּמצרתי סלעי (my rock, and my castle) in <reference osisRef="Ps.31.4">Psa 31:4</reference> as well (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.71.4">Psa 71:4</reference>). The two epithets are borrowed from the natural character of Palestine, where steep and almost inaccessible rocks afford protection to the fugitive, as David had often found at the time when Saul was pursuing him (vid., <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.22">1Sa 24:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.5">1Sa 22:5</reference>). But whilst David took refuge in rocks, he placed his hopes of safety not in their inaccessible character, but in God the Lord, the eternal spiritual rock, whom he could see in the earthly rock, so that he called Him his true castle. לי מפלטי (my deliverer to me) gives the real explanation of the foregoing figures. The לי (to me) is omitted in <reference osisRef="Ps.18.2">Psa 18:2</reference>, and only serves to strengthen the suffix, “my, yea <hi type="italic">my</hi> deliverer.' “<hi type="italic">My Rock-God</hi>,” equivalent to, God who is my Rock: this is formed after <reference osisRef="Deut.32.4">Deu 32:4</reference>, where Moses calls the Lord the Rock of Israel, because of His unchangeable faithfulness; for <hi type="italic">zur</hi>, a rock, is a figure used to represent immoveable firmness. In <reference osisRef="Ps.18.3">Psa 18:3</reference> we find צוּרי אלי, “my God” (strong one), “my rock,” two synonyms which are joined together in our text, so as to form one single predicate of God, which is repeated in 2Sa 22:47. The predicates which follow, “<hi type="italic">my horn and my salvation-shield</hi>,” describe God as the mighty protector and defender of the righteous. A shield covers against hostile attacks. In this respect God was Abraham’s shield (<reference osisRef="Gen.15.1">Gen 15:1</reference>), and the helping shield of Israel (<reference osisRef="Deut.33.29">Deu 33:29</reference>; cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.3.4">Psa 3:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.59.12">Psa 59:12</reference>). He is the “horn of salvation,” according to Luther, because He overcomes enemies, and rescues from foes, and gives salvation. The figure is borrowed from animals, which have their strength and defensive weapons in their horns (see at <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.1">1Sa 2:1</reference>). “<hi type="italic">My fortress:</hi>” <hi type="italic">misgab</hi> is a high place, where a person is secure against hostile attacks (see at <reference osisRef="Ps.9.10">Psa 9:10</reference>). The predicates which follow, viz., <hi type="italic">my refuge</hi>, etc., are not given in <reference osisRef="Ps.18.3">Psa 18:3</reference>, and are probably only added as a rhythmical completion to the strophe, which was shortened by the omission of the introductory lines, “I love thee heartily, Jehovah” (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.1">Psa 18:1</reference>). The last clause, “<hi type="italic">My Saviour, who redeemest me from violence,</hi>” corresponds to אחסה־בּו in the first hemistich. In <reference osisRef="Ps.18.4">Psa 18:4</reference>, David sums up the contents of his psalm of thanksgiving in a general sentence of experience, which may be called the theme of the psalm, for it embraces “the result of the long life which lay behind him, so full of dangers and deliverances.” מהלּל, “<hi type="italic">the praised one</hi>,” an epithet applied to God, which occurs several times in the Psalms (<reference osisRef="Ps.48.2">Psa 48:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.96.4">Psa 96:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.113.3">Psa 113:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.145.3">Psa 145:3</reference>). It is in apposition to Jehovah, and is placed first for the sake of emphasis: “I invoke Jehovah as the praised one.” The imperfects אקרא and אוּשׁע are used to denote what continually happens. In <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.5">2Sa 22:5</reference> we have the commencement of the account of the deliverances out of great tribulations, which David had experienced at the hand of God.
entries.9c9420632ee576265922a53ee25f0d83e96649f1: <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.5-2Sam.7.5">2Sa 22:5-7   5</reference>  For breakers of death had compassed me, <div eID="gen4568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4569" type="x-p"/> Streams of wickedness terrified me.   6  Cords of hell had girt me about, <div eID="gen4569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4570" type="x-p"/> Snares of death overtook me.   7  In my distress I called Jehovah, <div eID="gen4570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4571" type="x-p"/> And to my God I called; <div eID="gen4571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4572" type="x-p"/> And He heard my voice out of His temple, <div eID="gen4572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4573" type="x-p"/> And my crying came into His ears. <div eID="gen4573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4574" type="x-p"/> David had often been in danger of death, most frequently at the time when he was pursued by Saul, but also in Absalom’s conspiracy, and even in several wars (cf. <reference osisRef="2Sam.21.16">2Sa 21:16</reference>). All these dangers, out of which the Lord delivered him, and not merely those which originated with Saul, are included in <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.5">2Sa 22:5</reference>, 2Sa 22:6. The figure “<hi type="italic">breakers or waves of death</hi>” is analogous to that of the “<hi type="italic">streams of Belial</hi>.” His distress is represented in both of them under the image of violent floods of water. In the psalm we find מות חבלי, “snares of death,” as in <reference osisRef="Ps.116.3">Psa 116:3</reference>, death being regarded as a hunger with a net and snare (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.91.3">Psa 91:3</reference>): this does not answer to well to the parallel נחלי, and therefore is not so good, since שׁאול חבלי follows immediately. בליּעל (<hi type="italic">Belial</hi>), uselessness in a moral sense, or <hi type="italic">worthlessness</hi>. The meaning “mischief,” or injury in a physical sense, which many expositors give to the word in this passage on account of the parallel “death,” cannot be grammatically sustained. <hi type="italic">Belial</hi> was afterwards adopted as a name for the devil (<reference osisRef="2Cor.6.15">2Co 6:15</reference>). Streams of wickedness are calamities that proceed from wickedness, or originate with worthless men. קדּם, to come to meet with a hostile intention, i.e., to fall upon (vid., <reference osisRef="Job.30.27">Job 30:27</reference>). היכל, <hi type="italic">the temple</hi> out of which Jehovah heard him, was the heavenly abode of God, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.11.4">Psa 11:4</reference>; for, according to 2Sa 22:8., God came down from heaven to help him.
entries.a6f20a7ff73bfddf8fb658b4cf2c3bdb3838e364: <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.8-2Sam.10.8">2Sa 22:8-10   8</reference>  Then the earth swayed and trembled, <div eID="gen4574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4575" type="x-p"/> The foundations of the heavens shook <div eID="gen4575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4576" type="x-p"/> And swayed to and fro, because He was wroth.   9  Smoke ascended in His nose, <div eID="gen4576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4577" type="x-p"/> And fire out of His mouth devoured, <div eID="gen4577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4578" type="x-p"/> Red-hot coals burned out of Him. 10  And He bowed the heavens and came down, <div eID="gen4578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4579" type="x-p"/> And cloudy darkness under His feet. <div eID="gen4579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4580" type="x-p"/> Jehovah came down from heaven to save His servant, as He had formerly come down upon Sinai to conclude His covenant with Israel in the midst of terrible natural phenomena, which proclaimed the wrath of the Almighty. The theophany under which David depicts the deliverance he had experienced, had its type in the miraculous phenomenon which accompanied the descent of God upon Sinai, and which suggested, as in the song of Deborah (Jdg 5:4-5), the idea of a terrible storm. It is true that the deliverance of David was not actually attended by any such extraordinary natural phenomena; but the saving hand of God from heaven was so obviously manifested, that the deliverance experienced by him could be poetically described as a miraculous interposition on the part of God. When the Lord rises up from His heavenly temple to come down upon the earth to judgment, the whole world trembles at the fierceness of His wrath. Not only does the earth tremble, but the foundations of the heavens shake: the whole universe is moved. In the psalm we have “the foundations of the hills” instead of “<hi type="italic">the foundations of the heavens</hi>,” - a weaker expression, signifying the earth to its deepest foundations. The <hi type="italic">Hithpael</hi> יתגּעשׁ, lit., to <hi type="italic">sway itself</hi>, expresses the idea of continuous swaying to and fro. לו חרה כּי, “<hi type="italic">for it</hi> (sc., wrath) <hi type="italic">burned to him</hi>,” it flamed up like a fire; cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.32.22">Deu 32:22</reference>; Deu 29:19. <hi type="italic">“Smoke,”</hi> the forerunner of fire, “<hi type="italic">ascended in His nose</hi>.” The figurative idea is that of snorting or violent breathing, which indicates the rising of wrath. Smoke is followed by fire, which devours out of the mouth, i.e., bursts forth devouring or consuming all that opposes it. The expression is strengthened still further by the parallel: “<hi type="italic">red-hot coals come out of Him</hi>,” i.e., the flame of red-hot coals pours out of Him as out of a glowing furnace (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.15.17">Gen 15:17</reference>). This description is based entirely upon <reference osisRef="Exod.19.18">Exo 19:18</reference>, where the Lord comes down upon Sinai in smoke and fire. We are not to picture to ourselves flashes of lightning; for all these phenomena are merely the forerunners of the appearance of God in the clouds, which is described in <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.10">2Sa 22:10</reference>, “He bowed the heavens” to come down. ערפל, which is frequently connected with ענן, signifies cloudy darkness, or dark clouds. The substratum of this description is the fact that in a severe storm the heavens seem to sink down upon the earth with their dark clouds. The Lord draws near riding upon black thunder-clouds, “that the wicked may not behold His serene countenance, but only the terrible signs of His fierce wrath and punishment” (J. H. Michaelis).
entries.05286546aad8f2601c54856e4ea56158618ff13b: <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.11-2Sam.12.11">2Sa 22:11-12 11</reference>  He rode upon a cherub and flew hither, <div eID="gen4580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4581" type="x-p"/> And appeared upon the wings of the wind. 12  He made darkness round about Him as pavilions, <div eID="gen4581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4582" type="x-p"/> Water-gathering, thick clouds. 13  Out of the splendour before Him <div eID="gen4582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4583" type="x-p"/> Burned red-hot coals of fire. <div eID="gen4583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4584" type="x-p"/> These three verses are a further expansion of <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.19">2Sa 22:19</reference>, and <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.11">2Sa 22:11</reference> of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="2Sam.22.10">2Sa 22:10</reference></hi>. The <hi type="italic">cherub</hi> is not a personified earthly creature, for <hi type="italic">cherubim</hi> are angels around the throne of God (see at <reference osisRef="Gen.3.22">Gen 3:22</reference>). The poetical figure “riding upon the cherub” is borrowed from the fact that God was enthroned between the two cherubim upon the lid of the ark of the covenant, and above their outspread wings (<reference osisRef="Exod.25.20-Exod.25.21">Exo 25:20-21</reference>). As the idea of His “dwelling between the cherubim” (<reference osisRef="2Sam.6.2">2Sa 6:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.4.4">1Sa 4:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.80.2">Psa 80:2</reference>) was founded upon this typical manifestation of the gracious presence of God in the Most Holy place, so here David depicts the descent of Jehovah from heaven as “riding upon a cherub,” picturing the cherub as a throne upon which God appears in the clouds of heaven, though without therefore imagining Him as riding upon a sphinx or driving in a chariot-throne. Such notions as these are precluded by the addition of the term ויּעף, “did fly.” The “<hi type="italic">flying</hi>” is also suggested by the wings of the cherubim. As the divine “<hi type="italic">shechinah</hi>” was enthroned above the ark of the covenant upon the wings of the cherubim, David in his poetical description represents the cherub and his wings as carrying the throne of God, to express the thought that Jehovah came down from heaven as the judge and saviour of His servants in the splendour of His divine glory, surrounded by cherubim who stand as His highest servants around His throne, just as Moses in his blessing (<reference osisRef="Deut.33.2">Deu 33:2</reference>) speaks of Jehovah as coming out of myriads of His holy angels. The elementary substratum of this was the wings of the wind, upon which He appeared. In the psalm we have ויּדא, from דּאה, to soar (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.39">Deu 28:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.48.40">Jer 48:40</reference>), which suggests the idea of flying better than ויּרא (He was seen), though the latter gives the real explanation. In <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.12">2Sa 22:12</reference> and <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.13">2Sa 22:13</reference>, the “cloudy darkness under His feet” (<hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="2Sam.22.10">2Sa 22:10</reference></hi>) is still further expanded, so as to prepare the way for the description of thunder and lightning in 2Sa 22:14. God in His wrath withdraws His face from man. He envelopes himself in clouds. The darkness round about him is the black thunder-cloud which forms His hut or tent. The plural <hi type="italic">succoth</hi> is occasioned by the plural סביבתיו, “His surroundings:” it is used with indefinite generality, and is more probably the original term than סכּתו in the psalm. The “<hi type="italic">darkness</hi>” is still further explained in the second clause, מים חשׁרת, <hi type="italic">water-gatherings</hi>. חשׁרה (ἁπ. λεγ.) signifies, according to the Arabic, a gathering or collection. The expression used in the psalm is מים חשׁכת, <hi type="italic">water-darkness</hi>, which, if not less appropriate, is at any rate not the original term. שׁחקים עבי, <hi type="italic">clouds of clouds</hi>, i.e., the thickest clouds; a kind of superlative, in which a synonym is used instead of the same noun.
entries.afd9d306e260bcbf9e4b2b76d9b93cae9a3e532c: <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.13">2Sa 22:13</reference> <div eID="gen4584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4585" type="x-p"/> The splendour of the divine nature enveloped in clouds breaks through the dark covering in burning coals of fire. The coals of fire which burst forth, i.e., which break out in flame from the dark clouds, are the lightning which shoots forth from the dark storm-clouds in streams of fire.
entries.71de03769855876ec3eaa048b163f6a0594f22a4: 2 Sa22:14-16 <div eID="gen4585" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen4586"/> <l level="1" sID="gen4587"/>14  Jehovah thundered from the heavens,<l eID="gen4587" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen4588"/>And the Most High gave His voice. 15  He sent arrows, and scattered them;<l eID="gen4588" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen4589"/>Lightning, and discomfited them. 16  Then the beds of the sea became visible;<l eID="gen4589" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen4590"/>The foundations of the world were uncovered,<l eID="gen4590" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen4591"/>Through the threatening of Jehovah,<l eID="gen4591" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen4592"/>By the snorting of the breath of His nostrils.<l eID="gen4592" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen4586"/> <div sID="gen4593" type="x-p"/> God sent lightning as arrows upon the enemies along with violent thunder, and threw them thereby into confusion. המם, to throw into confusion, and thereby to destroy, is the standing expression for the destruction of the foe accomplished by the miraculous interposition of God (vid., <reference osisRef="Exod.14.24">Exo 14:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.23.27">Exo 23:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.10.10">Jos 10:10</reference>; Jdg 4:15; <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.10">1Sa 7:10</reference>). To the thunder there were added stormy wind and earthquake, as an effect of the wrath of God, whereby the foundations of the sea and land were laid bare, i.e., whereby the depth of the abyss and of the hell in the interior of the earth, into which the person to be rescued had fallen, were disclosed.<note placement="foot">In <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.13-2Sam.22.16">2Sa 22:13-16</reference> the text of the Psalms deviates greatly and in many instances from that before us. In v. 13 we find אשׁ וגחלי בּרד עברוּ עביו instead of אשׁ גּחלי בּערוּ; and after v. 14 אשׁ וגחלי בּרד is repeated in the psalm. In v. 15 we have רב וּברקים for בּרק, and in v. 16 מים אפיקי for ים אפיקי. The other deviations are inconsiderable. So far as the repetition of אשׁ וגחלי בּרד at the end of v. 14 is concerned, it is not only superfluous, but unsuitable, because the lightning following the thunder is described in v. 15, and the words repeated are probably nothing more than a gloss that has crept by an oversight into the text. The מים אפיקי in v. 16 is an obvious softening down of the ים אפיקי of the text before us. In the other deviations, however, the text of the Psalms is evidently the more original of the two; the abridgment of the second clause of v. 13 is evidently a simplification of the figurative description in the psalm, and רב בּרקים in the 15th verse of the psalm is more poetical and a stronger expression than the mere בּרק of our text.</note>
entries.688b8cb529ba3badaa2a8e0ed1c70266c4717602: <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.17-2Sam.20.17">2Sa 22:17-20 17</reference>  He reached out of the height, He laid hold of me; <div eID="gen4593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4594" type="x-p"/> Drew me out of great waters: 18  Saved me from my enemy strong; <div eID="gen4594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4595" type="x-p"/> From my haters, because they were too strong for me. 19  They fell upon me in my day of calamity: <div eID="gen4595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4596" type="x-p"/> Then Jehovah became my stay, 20  And led me out into a broad place; <div eID="gen4596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4597" type="x-p"/> Delivered me, because He had pleasure in me. <div eID="gen4597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4598" type="x-p"/> The Lord stretched His hand from the height into the deep abysses, which had been uncovered through the threatening of the wrath of God, and drew out the sinking man. ישׁלח without יד is used to denote the stretching out of the hand, and in the sense of reaching out to a thing (as in <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.6">2Sa 6:6</reference>). רבּים מים (great waters) does not refer to the enemy, but to the calamities and dangers (waves of death and streams of Belial, <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.5">2Sa 22:5</reference>) into which the enemies of the Psalmist had plunged him. ימשׁני, from משׁה (<reference osisRef="Exod.2.10">Exo 2:10</reference>), from which the name of <hi type="italic">Moses</hi> was derived, to whom there is probably an allusion made. As Moses was taken out of the waters of the Nile, so David was taken out of great (many) waters. This deliverance is still further depicted in a more literal terms in 2Sa 22:18. עז איבי, my enemy strong, poetical for my strong enemy, does not refer to one single enemy, namely Saul; but, as the parallel “my haters” shows, is a poetical personification of all his enemies. They were stronger than David, therefore the Lord had to deliver him with an almighty hand. The “<hi type="italic">day of calamity</hi>” in which the enemy fell upon him (קדּם: see at <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.6">2Sa 22:6</reference>) was the time when David wandered about in the desert helpless and homeless, fleeing from the pursuit of Saul. The Lord was then his support, or a staff on which he could support himself (vid., <reference osisRef="Ps.23.4">Psa 23:4</reference>), and led him out of the strait into the broad, i.e., into a broad space where he could move freely, because God had pleasure in him, and had chosen him in His grace to be His servant. This reason for his deliverance is carried out still further in what follows.
entries.ea7d59370521c70494175f4c2a31f6d32918193e: 2Sa 22:21-24 21  Jehovah rendered to me according to my righteousness, <div eID="gen4598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4599" type="x-p"/> According to the cleanness of my hands He recompensed me. 22  For I have observed the ways of Jehovah, <div eID="gen4599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4600" type="x-p"/> And have not wickedly departed from my God. 23  For all His rights are before my eyes; <div eID="gen4600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4601" type="x-p"/> And His statutes,-I do not depart from them. 24  And I was innocent towards Him, <div eID="gen4601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4602" type="x-p"/> And kept myself from mine iniquity. גּמל signifies to do to a person good or evil, like the Greek εὖ and κακῶς πράττειν τινά. The <hi type="italic">righteousness</hi> and <hi type="italic">cleanness of hands</hi>, i.e., the innocence, which David attributed to himself, were not perfect righteousness or holiness before God, but the righteousness of his endeavours and deeds as contrasted with the unrighteousness and wickedness of his adversaries and pursuers, and consisted in the fact that he endeavoured earnestly and sincerely to walk in the ways of God and to keep the divine commandments. מן רשׁע, <hi type="italic">to be wicked from</hi>, is a pregnant expression, signifying to depart wickedly from God. לנגדּי, i.e., as a standard before my eye. In the psalm we find עמּו תמים, innocent in intercourse with the Lord, instead of לו תמים (see <reference osisRef="Deut.18.13">Deu 18:13</reference>); and for the fact itself, David’s own testimony in <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.23-1Sam.26.24">1Sa 26:23-24</reference>, the testimony of God concerning him in 1Ki 14:8, and the testimony of history in 1Ki 15:5. מעוני, from mine iniquity, i.e., from the iniquity which I might have committed.
entries.46e9c6ccc803e3edf20a69326d4084e42db51fc5: 2Sa 22:25-28 25  Thus Jehovah repaid me according to my righteousness, <div eID="gen4602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4603" type="x-p"/> According to my cleanness before His eyes. 26  Towards the pious Thou showest thyself pious, <div eID="gen4603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4604" type="x-p"/> Towards the perfectly innocent Thou showest thyself innocent. 27  Towards the genuine Thou showest thyself genuine, <div eID="gen4604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4605" type="x-p"/> And towards the perverse Thou showest thyself crooked. 28  And afflicted people Thou helpest, <div eID="gen4605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4606" type="x-p"/> And Thine eyes are against the haughty; them Thou humblest. <div eID="gen4606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4607" type="x-p"/> The motive for deliverance, which was expounded in <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.21-2Sam.22.24">2Sa 22:21-24</reference>, is summed up briefly in <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.25">2Sa 22:25</reference>; and then in <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.26">2Sa 22:26</reference> and <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.27">2Sa 22:27</reference> it is carried back to the general truth, that the conduct of God towards men is regulated according to the conduct of men towards God. The <hi type="italic">vav cons</hi>. in ויּשׁב expresses the logical consequence. כּברי is used instead of ידי כּבר in <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.21">2Sa 22:21</reference>, which is repeated in the psalm simply for the sake of variation. The truth that God treats every man in accordance with his conduct towards Him, is expounded in four parallel clauses, in which the conduct of God is expressed in verbs in the <hi type="italic">Hithpael</hi>, formed from the adjectives used to describe the conduct of men towards God. To the חסיד, the pious or devoted to God, He also shows himself pious; and innocent, blameless, to the תמים גּבּור, the man strong in innocence, who walks in perfect innocence. נבר, a <hi type="italic">Niphal</hi> participle, from בּרר, he who keeps himself pure, strives after purity of walk. תּתּבר, an anomalous contraction of תּתבּרר (Ps.), analogous to the formation of נבר for נברר. The form תּתּפּל for תּתפּתּל, to show one’s self perverse of crooked, is still more anomalous. God shows himself so towards the perverse, by giving him up to his perverseness (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.28">Rom 1:28</reference>). This general truth is applied in <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.28">2Sa 22:28</reference> to the congregation of God, in the contrast which it presents of humble and haughty, and is expounded from the conduct of God, as displayed in the history of Israel, towards these two classes of men, into which the nation was divided. In the psalm, therefore, we find אתּה כּי, for which the simple ו is substituted here, because the verse does not contain any actual reason for what goes before. עני עם, afflicted people, is used to denote the pious and depressed in the nation; רמים, <hi type="italic">the high</hi>, i.e., the haughty, or godless rich and mighty in the nation. תּשׁפּיל is to be taken as a relative: whom Thou humblest (see Ewald, §332, <hi type="italic">b</hi>.; and for the thought, <reference osisRef="Isa.2.11">Isa 2:11</reference>). In the psalm the unusual mode of expression in the second clause is changed into the more common phrase, “Thou bringest down high, i.e., proud looks” (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.6.17">Pro 6:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.21.4">Pro 21:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.30.13">Pro 30:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.131.1">Psa 131:1</reference>, etc.). <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.29">2Sa 22:29</reference> commences the description of the help which David had already received from God in his conflict with the enemies of Israel, and which he would still receive. 29  For Thou art my lamp, O Jehovah! <div eID="gen4607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4608" type="x-p"/> And Jehovah maketh my darkness bright. 30  For through Thee I run troops, <div eID="gen4608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4609" type="x-p"/> And through my God I leap walls. 31  God - innocent is His way. <div eID="gen4609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4610" type="x-p"/> The word of Jehovah is refined, <div eID="gen4610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4611" type="x-p"/> A shield is He to all who trust in Him. <div eID="gen4611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4612" type="x-p"/> The explanatory כּי, with which the new description of the divine mercy commences, refers to the thought implied in <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.28">2Sa 22:28</reference>, that David belonged to the “afflicted people,” whom the Lord always helps. As the Lord delivered him out of the danger of death, because He took pleasure in him, so He also gave him power over all his enemies. For He was his lamp, i.e., He had lifted him out of a condition of depression and contempt into one of glory and honour (see at <reference osisRef="2Sam.21.17">2Sa 21:17</reference>), and would still further enlighten his darkness, i.e., “would cause the light of His salvation to shine upon him and his tribe in all the darkness of their distress” (<hi type="italic">Hengstenberg</hi>). In the psalm the verse reads thus: “For Thou lightest (makest bright) my lamp (or candle), Jehovah my God enlighteneth my darkness;” the bold figure “Jehovah the lamp of David” being more literally explained. The figure is analogous to the one in <reference osisRef="Ps.27.1">Psa 27:1</reference>, “The Lord is my light;” whilst the form ניר is a later mode of writing נר.
entries.4ae4b4491a8d5c850dc7510ba7b3f5898e9bf829: <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.30">2Sa 22:30</reference> <div eID="gen4612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4613" type="x-p"/> In the strength of his God he could run hostile troops and leap walls, i.e., overcome every hostile power. ארוּץ, not from רצץ, to smash in pieces, but from רוּץ, to run; construed with the accusative according to the analogy of verbs of motion.
entries.a6680e0c008e2292a92593a927cd2fc3e1b8bc6d: <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.31">2Sa 22:31</reference> <div eID="gen4613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4614" type="x-p"/> He derives this confidence from the acts of God, and also from His word. האל (God) is written absolutely, like הצּוּר in Deu 32:4. The article points back to בּאלהי. Jehovah is <hi type="italic">the</hi> God (האל), whose way is perfect, without blemish; and His word is refined brass, pure silver (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.12.7">Psa 12:7</reference>). He who trusts in Him is safe from all foes. The last two clauses occur again in Agur’s proverbs (<reference osisRef="Prov.30.5">Pro 30:5</reference>). The thought of the last clause is still further explained in 2Sa 22:32.
entries.fa246541db525645d490ebb373d02d57427c038d: 2Sa 22:32-35 32  For who is God save Jehovah, <div eID="gen4614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4615" type="x-p"/> And who a rock save our God? 33  This God is my strong fortress, <div eID="gen4615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4616" type="x-p"/> And leads the innocent his way. 34  He makes my feet like the hinds, <div eID="gen4616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4617" type="x-p"/> And setteth me upon my high places; 35  He teacheth my hands to fight, <div eID="gen4617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4618" type="x-p"/> And my arms span brazen bows. <div eID="gen4618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4619" type="x-p"/> There is no true God who can help, except or by the side of Jehovah (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.32.31">Deu 32:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.2">1Sa 2:2</reference>). צוּר, as in 2Sa 22:2. This God is “my strong fortress:” for this figure, comp. <reference osisRef="Ps.31.5">Psa 31:5</reference> and Psa 27:1. חיל, strength, might, is construed with מעוּזי, by free subordination: “my fortress, a strong one,” like עז מחסי (<reference osisRef="Ps.71.7">Psa 71:7</reference>; cf. Ewald, §291, <hi type="italic">b</hi>.). יתּר for יתר, from תּוּר (vid., Ges<hi type="italic">.</hi> §72; Olshausen, <hi type="italic">Gram</hi>. p. 579), in the sense of leading or taking round, as in Pro 12:26. God leads the innocent his way, i.e., He is his leader and guide therein. The <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> דּרכּי rests upon a misunderstanding. There is an important difference in the reading of this verse in Ps 18, viz., “The God who girdeth me with strength, and makes my way innocent.” The last clause is certainly an alteration which simplifies the meaning, and so is also the first clause, the thought of which occurs again, word for word, in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="2Sam.22.40">2Sa 22:40</reference></hi>, with the addition of למּלחמה. איּלה or איּלת, the hind, or female stag, is a figure of speech denoting swiftness in running. “<hi type="italic">Like the hinds:</hi>” a condensed simile for “like the hinds’ feet,” such as we frequently meet with in Hebrew (vid., <hi type="italic">Ges.</hi> §144, Anm.). The reference is to swiftness in pursuit of the foe (vid., <reference osisRef="2Sam.2.18">2Sa 2:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.8">1Ch 12:8</reference>). רגליו, <hi type="italic">his</hi> feet, for רגלי (<hi type="italic">my</hi> feet) in the psalm, may be accounted for from the fact, that David had spoken of himself in the third person as the innocent one. “<hi type="italic">My high places</hi>” were not the high places of the enemy, that became his by virtue of conquest, but the high places of his own land, which he maintained triumphantly, so that he ruled the land for them. The expression is formed after <reference osisRef="Deut.32.13">Deu 32:13</reference>, and is imitated in Hab 3:19. למּד is generally construed with a double accusative: here it is written with an accusative and ל, and signifies to instruct for the war. נחת, in the psalm נחתה, on account of the feminine זרועתי, is not the <hi type="italic">Niphal</hi> of חתת, to be broken in pieces, but the <hi type="italic">Piel</hi> of נחת, to cause to go down, to press down the bow, i.e., to set it. The bow of brass is mentioned as being the strongest: setting such a bow would be a sign of great heroic strength. The two verses (<reference osisRef="2Sam.22.34">2Sa 22:34</reference> and <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.35">2Sa 22:35</reference>) are simply a particularizing description of the power and might with which the Lord had endowed David to enable him to conquer all his foes.
entries.e706504077a11202eb022f372a0e32cca5e71517: 2Sa 22:36-37 36  And Thou reachest me the shield of my salvation, <div eID="gen4619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4620" type="x-p"/> And Thy hearing makes me great. 37  Thou makest my steps broad under me, <div eID="gen4620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4621" type="x-p"/> And my ankles have not trembled. <div eID="gen4621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4622" type="x-p"/> The Lord bestows the true strength for victory in His salvation. The shield of salvation is the shield which consists of salvation, of the helping grace of the Lord. ענתך, for which we find in the psalm ענותך, thy humility, i.e., God’s condescending grace, does not mean “thy humiliation,” but “<hi type="italic">thy hearkening</hi>,” i.e., that practical hearkening on the part of God, when called upon for help, which was manifested in the fact that God made his steps broad, i.e., provided the walker with a broad space for free motion, removing obstructions and stumbling-blocks out of the way. God had done this for David, so that his ankles had not trembled, i.e., he had not been wanting in the power to take firm and safe steps. In this strength of his God he could destroy all his foes.
